Sad sack
SAD sak
noun (Silent Generation slang)
Army slang of the Second World War. A cruder barracks phrase lay behind it among American soldiers of the early 1940s; the clean form was made famous by The Sad Sack, the cartoon strip Sergeant George Baker drew for Yank, the Army Weekly from 1942 — a wordless, put-upon private who could never get anything right. By war’s end sad sack meant any hapless, inept, perpetually unlucky fellow, in uniform or out.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

To a soldier in 1943, a sad sack was the private whose boots were never shined, whose rifle was dirty at inspection, who drew KP every week and somehow fell in the mud on the way back. Sergeant Baker’s cartoon made him lovable, and every man in the barracks recognized a little of himself in him. Grandpa used the word with a grin: "Poor fellow, he’s a real sad sack." Scripture has a great deal to say about the sad sack, and most of it is good news. The Lord does not pick His people for their polish: "God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty" (1Co 1:27). He is not surprised by our clumsiness, "For he knoweth our frame; he remembereth that we are dust" (Psa 103:14). Of Christ it was promised, "A bruised reed shall he not break, and the smoking flax shall he not quench" (Isa 42:3). The apostle Paul learned to hear the Lord’s word over his own weakness: "My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness" (2Co 12:9). So the Christian can enjoy the joke and still refuse the sneer. The man who always gets it wrong is exactly the man Jesus calls: "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest" (Mat 11:28). Grandpa’s barracks had a sad sack, and so does every family. Be the one who helps him lace his boots.

Webster 1828 Definition

Silent Generation slang (WWII Army, 1940s; made famous by the Yank cartoon) for a hapless, inept, perpetually unlucky fellow — the very kind of weak man God delights to choose, whose strength is made perfect in weakness (2Co 12:9).

SAD SACK, n. (Silent Generation slang, 1940s; WWII Army) A hapless, inept, perpetually unlucky person; a well-meaning blunderer. "He’s a good kid, but a real sad sack on the drill field."

Decode for families: laugh with the sad sack, never at him — Christ came for exactly that man.

Key Scripture

1Co 1:27 — "But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty;"

Psa 103:14 — "For he knoweth our frame; he remembereth that we are dust."

Isa 42:3 — "A bruised reed shall he not break, and the smoking flax shall he not quench: he shall bring forth judgment unto truth."

2Co 12:9 — "And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me."

Mat 11:28 — "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest."

Modern Corruption

Mostly a fond joke; the danger is only when the label hardens into contempt for a weaker brother whom Christ has not despised.

expand to see more

There is little to correct in sad sack. The soldiers who read Baker’s strip laughed at the Sack because they saw themselves in him; the joke was a kind of fellowship among tired, homesick men who all fell short of regulation. Laughing together at our own clumsiness is a healthy thing, and humility can wear a grin.

The word turns sour when it stops being shared and becomes a verdict on someone else — the boy who is always picked last, the coworker everyone sighs about. Scripture forbids that contempt: the Lord who will not break a bruised reed (Isa 42:3) does not let His people break one either. A Christian family can keep the word as a gentle joke and refuse it as a sneer.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Barracks slang (early 1940s) → The Sad Sack cartoon in Yank (1942) → general American slang for a hapless blunderer → Silent Generation household word.

expand to see more

sad — Old English sæd, sated, weary; later sorrowful, pitiable

sack — a bag; in slang, a shapeless, slumped figure (compare sack of potatoes)

Early 1940s: Army barracks phrase for a hopeless soldier

1942: The Sad Sack, Sgt. George Baker’s wordless private in Yank, the Army Weekly

Postwar: any well-meaning, luckless blunderer

Usage

""Your great-uncle Walt was the sad sack of his whole company — and the bravest man I ever knew.""

"My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness (2Co 12:9)."

"For he knoweth our frame; he remembereth that we are dust (Psa 103:14)."
